bio.topic: Enzymes: effects of temperature and pH

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: What is the optimum temperature for most human enzymes?
questions.hint: Think of normal human body temperature.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Give the term for the permanent change in the shape of an enzyme's active site caused by high temperature or extreme pH.
questions.hint: The enzyme is said to be de…

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Which part of an enzyme changes shape when it is denatured?
questions.hint: It is the region where the substrate binds.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Why does the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction increase from 10 °C to 30 °C?
options: Molecules gain kinetic energy and collide more often
questions.answer: Molecules gain kinetic energy and collide more often
questions.hint: Think about collisions between enzyme and substrate.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: What is the approximate optimum pH of pepsin, a protease in the stomach?
questions.hint: The stomach contains hydrochloric acid.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: What is the approximate optimum pH of salivary amylase?
questions.hint: Saliva is close to neutral.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Why can a denatured enzyme no longer catalyse its reaction?
options: The substrate no longer fits the active site
The enzyme has been used up
questions.answer: The substrate no longer fits the active site
questions.hint: Think of the lock and key model.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: In an investigation, amylase fully digested starch in 40 s. Calculate the rate using rate = 1000 ÷ time (s).
questions.hint: Divide 1000 by the time taken.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: At 30 °C, catalase produced 24 cm³ of oxygen in 2 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of oxygen production in cm³ per minute.
questions.hint: Volume ÷ time.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Which test result shows that starch is still present in an amylase investigation?
questions.hint: Iodine is the test for starch.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: In an investigation into the effect of pH on amylase, what is the independent variable?
questions.hint: It is the variable you deliberately change.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Name the apparatus used to keep a reaction mixture at a constant temperature.
questions.hint: It is usually electric and thermostatically controlled.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Why does an extreme pH reduce enzyme activity?
options: It disrupts the bonds that hold the active site in shape
It gives molecules more kinetic energy
questions.answer: It disrupts the bonds that hold the active site in shape
questions.hint: Think about the enzyme's 3D structure.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Explain why the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction decreases rapidly above the optimum temperature.
questions.hint: Refer to bonds, the active site and enzyme–substrate complexes.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Describe how you could investigate the effect of pH on the activity of amylase.
questions.hint: Include buffers, a water bath, iodine on a spotting tile and timing.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Which variable must be controlled when investigating the effect of pH on enzyme activity?
questions.hint: Which other factor in this topic changes enzyme activity?

bss.topic: Ditadura civil-militar: Atos Institucionais e repressão

questions.q: Em que ano começou a ditadura civil-militar no Brasil?

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual Ato Institucional é considerado o mais duro da ditadura?
questions.hint: Foi decretado no fim de 1968.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Em que ano foi decretado o AI-5?

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Como se chama o controle do governo sobre jornais, músicas, filmes e peças antes de serem divulgados?
questions.hint: Ela impedia a livre expressão.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: O que eram os Atos Institucionais?

questions.hint: Eram usados para ampliar o poder do Executivo.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: O que eram os DOI-CODI?
questions.hint: Estavam ligados às Forças Armadas.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Por que muitos historiadores usam o termo "ditadura civil-militar"?
options: Porque o regime teve apoio e participação de setores civis, como empresários e parte da imprensa
Porque os presidentes eram eleitos pelo voto popular

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: O AI-5 permitiu ao presidente fazer o quê com o Congresso Nacional?

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Em que ano foi aprovada a Lei da Anistia no Brasil?
questions.hint: Foi um passo da abertura política, no fim da década de 1970.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual era o objetivo da Comissão Nacional da Verdade (2012–2014)?
options: Investigar graves violações de direitos humanos cometidas por agentes do Estado
questions.answer: Investigar graves violações de direitos humanos cometidas por agentes do Estado

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: O que o habeas corpus garante?
options: Que ninguém seja preso ou mantido preso ilegalmente
questions.answer: Que ninguém seja preso ou mantido preso ilegalmente

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual documento internacional, de 1948, já proibia a tortura antes do golpe?
questions.hint: Foi aprovado pela ONU após a Segunda Guerra Mundial.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Explique por que a censura é considerada uma ameaça à democracia.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Analise como o AI-5 aumentou o poder do Executivo e reduziu os direitos dos cidadãos.

bus.topic: Motivating employees: importance and Maslow's hierarchy of needs

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: What is meant by 'motivation' at work?
options: The factors that make people want to work well
The amount of money a business makes
The number of hours an employee works
The training given to new workers
questions.answer: The factors that make people want to work well
questions.hint: Think about what drives a worker's effort.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which of these is most likely to be a result of a well-motivated workforce?
questions.hint: Motivated workers are less likely to want to leave.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: What term describes the rate at which employees leave a business and have to be replaced?
questions.hint: It is measured as a percentage of the workforce.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: What is absenteeism?
options: Workers regularly being away from work without a good reason
Workers leaving to join a competitor
questions.answer: Workers regularly being away from work without a good reason
questions.hint: Think about being absent.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which level is at the bottom of Maslow's hierarchy of needs?
questions.hint: These are the most basic needs for survival.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which level is at the top of Maslow's hierarchy of needs?
questions.hint: It is about reaching your full potential.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Put in order from lowest to highest: which level comes directly above safety needs in Maslow's hierarchy?
questions.hint: After feeling secure, people want to belong.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A business offers employees a permanent contract and a pension scheme. Which of Maslow's needs is it mainly meeting?
questions.hint: Think about job security.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A business introduces team-building days and a staff canteen where workers eat together. Which need is it mainly meeting?
questions.hint: Think about friendship and belonging.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: An 'Employee of the Month' award and a job title promotion mainly meet which level of Maslow's hierarchy?
questions.hint: Think about recognition and status.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which of these would best help a worker reach self-actualisation?
options: Challenging work that lets them develop their full potential
A locker to keep belongings safe
questions.answer: Challenging work that lets them develop their full potential
questions.hint: This is the highest level of the hierarchy.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: According to Maslow, what usually happens once a lower level of need is satisfied?
options: It no longer motivates, and the next level becomes the motivator
The worker stops being motivated at all
The worker moves back down to the bottom level
questions.answer: It no longer motivates, and the next level becomes the motivator
questions.hint: Think about why the theory is drawn as a hierarchy.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A firm had 6 employees leave in a year and an average workforce of 120. Calculate the labour turnover as a percentage.
questions.hint: Divide the number of leavers by the average number of staff, then multiply by 100.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which is a limitation of Maslow's hierarchy for managers?
options: Not every worker's needs follow the same order
It says pay is the only motivator
questions.answer: Not every worker's needs follow the same order
questions.hint: Think about how individuals differ.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Explain two reasons why it is important for a business to have motivated employees.
questions.hint: Think about productivity, costs of recruitment and customer service.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A fast-food restaurant pays the minimum wage and has high labour turnover. Using Maslow's hierarchy, explain how the manager could improve motivation.
questions.hint: Choose specific levels of the hierarchy and suggest a practical action for each.

chem.topic: Molar gas volume and concentration of solutions

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: What is the volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.)?
questions.hint: This value is the same for every gas.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: How many cm³ are there in 1 dm³?
questions.hint: A cube with 10 cm sides has a volume of 1 dm³.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Convert 250 cm³ into dm³.
questions.hint: Divide by the number of cm³ in one dm³.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Calculate the volume, in dm³, occupied by 0.5 mol of carbon dioxide at r.t.p.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of moles by the molar gas volume.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Calculate the number of moles of gas in 48 dm³ of nitrogen at r.t.p.
questions.hint: Divide the volume by the molar gas volume.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Calculate the volume, in cm³, of 0.1 mol of hydrogen gas at r.t.p.
questions.hint: Use the molar gas volume in cm³.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Calculate the volume, in dm³, occupied by 8 g of oxygen gas, O₂, at r.t.p. (Ar: O = 16)
questions.hint: First find the number of moles using mass ÷ Mr.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: In a solution of salt in water, what is the salt called?
questions.hint: It is the substance that dissolves.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which unit is used for concentration measured in moles?
questions.hint: Concentration is an amount per unit volume.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: 0.2 mol of sodium chloride is dissolved in water to make 500 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³.
questions.hint: Convert the volume into dm³ first.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: 5 g of a solute is dissolved to make 250 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in g/dm³.
questions.hint: Concentration = mass ÷ volume in dm³.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Calculate the number of moles of solute in 25.0 cm³ of a 0.200 mol/dm³ solution.
questions.hint: Moles = concentration × volume in dm³.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Calculate the mass, in g, of sodium hydroxide (Mr = 40) needed to make 250 cm³ of a 0.1 mol/dm³ solution.
questions.hint: Find the moles first, then multiply by Mr.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: A solution of hydrochloric acid has a concentration of 2 mol/dm³. Calculate its concentration in g/dm³. (Mr of HCl = 36.5)
questions.hint: Multiply the concentration in mol/dm³ by Mr.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: 10 g of calcium carbonate (Mr = 100) reacts with excess acid: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the volume of CO₂, in dm³, produced at r.t.p.
questions.hint: Use the mole ratio of CaCO₃ to CO₂ from the equation.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Explain why 1 mol of oxygen and 1 mol of helium occupy the same volume at r.t.p., even though their molecules have different masses.
questions.hint: Think about the number of particles and the spaces between gas particles.

comp.topic: Algorithm design: the program development life cycle and decomposition

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What are the four stages of the program development life cycle?
questions.hint: It starts by understanding the problem.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: In which stage of the program development life cycle are the requirements of the problem identified?
questions.hint: This happens before any solution is planned.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: In which stage are structure diagrams, flowcharts and pseudocode produced?
questions.hint: These show how the solution will work before it is written.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: In which stage is the program written in a programming language?
questions.hint: This stage produces the actual program.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What is the purpose of the testing stage?
options: To check the program works correctly using test data
To decide what the problem is
questions.answer: To check the program works correctly using test data
questions.hint: Think about finding errors.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What term describes breaking a complex problem down into smaller, more manageable parts?
questions.hint: It is a key part of computational thinking.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What term describes removing unnecessary details from a problem so you can focus on what is important?
questions.hint: A map of a train network that ignores real distances is an example.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What type of diagram shows a problem broken down into sub-systems in a hierarchy?
questions.hint: It looks like a tree, with the whole system at the top.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: When decomposing a problem, what are the four component parts usually identified?
questions.hint: Think about what goes in, what happens, what comes out and what is kept.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A program calculates the average of five test marks typed in by a teacher. Which is an INPUT?
questions.hint: Inputs are the data entered into the system.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: In the same average-mark program, which is a PROCESS?
options: Adding the marks and dividing by five
questions.answer: Adding the marks and dividing by five
questions.hint: A process is what the program does with the data.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: In the same program, which is an OUTPUT?
options: The average displayed on the screen
questions.answer: The average displayed on the screen
questions.hint: Outputs are the results given back to the user.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A library system keeps records of all the books borrowed so they can be checked later. Which component of the system does this describe?
questions.hint: The data is kept for later use.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Why is a problem decomposed before it is coded?
options: Smaller parts are easier to understand, write and test
It makes the program run faster
It removes the need for testing
It stops the program needing inputs
questions.answer: Smaller parts are easier to understand, write and test
questions.hint: Think about working in a team on a big project.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A school wants a program that records students' lunch orders and prints a daily total for the kitchen. Identify one input, one process, one output and one item of storage for this system.
questions.hint: Think about what is typed in, what is calculated, what is printed and what is kept.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Describe what happens in the analysis stage of the program development life cycle.
questions.hint: Think about understanding the problem and what the solution must do.

econ.topic: Market failure: public goods, merit goods and demerit goods

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What term describes a situation where the free market fails to allocate resources efficiently?
questions.hint: The market does not produce the best outcome for society.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which pair of characteristics defines a public good?
questions.hint: Think about whether people can be stopped from using it, and whether one person's use reduces another's.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which of these is the best example of a public good?
questions.hint: Everyone walking along the road benefits from it.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What does 'non-excludable' mean?
options: People cannot be stopped from benefiting even if they do not pay
Only one person can use the good at a time
The good is produced by the government
questions.answer: People cannot be stopped from benefiting even if they do not pay
questions.hint: Think about whether a firm could charge everyone who benefits.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What does 'non-rival' mean?
options: One person's use does not reduce the amount available to others
Firms do not compete to sell the good
The good is free to produce
questions.answer: One person's use does not reduce the amount available to others
questions.hint: Think about whether consumption 'uses up' the good.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What name is given to someone who benefits from a good without paying for it?
questions.hint: They 'ride' along at no cost.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Why will private firms usually not provide public goods?
options: They cannot make people pay, so they cannot make a profit
Public goods are illegal for firms to sell
There is no demand for public goods
Public goods are too cheap to produce
questions.answer: They cannot make people pay, so they cannot make a profit
questions.hint: Think about the free rider problem.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What is a merit good?
options: A good that is under-consumed in a free market and benefits society
A good that is over-consumed and harms society
A good that is non-excludable and non-rival
A good bought only by rich people
questions.answer: A good that is under-consumed in a free market and benefits society
questions.hint: People do not always realise how much it benefits them.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which of these is an example of a merit good?
questions.hint: It benefits both the individual and society.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which of these is an example of a demerit good?
questions.hint: It harms the consumer and others.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: In a free market, demerit goods tend to be…
questions.hint: Consumers may not consider the full harm.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: One reason merit goods are under-consumed is that consumers…
options: know exactly how useful they are
are not allowed to buy them
questions.hint: Think about information failure.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which government policy would most likely reduce consumption of a demerit good?
options: An indirect tax on the good
A subsidy to producers of the good
Lowering the price of the good
questions.answer: An indirect tax on the good
questions.hint: Think about what happens to demand when price rises.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which government policy would most likely increase consumption of a merit good?
questions.hint: This lowers costs for producers.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Explain why a lighthouse is considered a public good.
questions.hint: Use both key characteristics of public goods in your answer.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Explain why the free market may under-provide vaccinations, and suggest one way the government could correct this.
questions.hint: Think about benefits to other people and about information.

en.topic: Non-fiction text types: articles, reviews and discursive essays

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which non-fiction form usually gives an opinion on a film, book or product and often ends with a rating or recommendation?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What is the main purpose of a discursive essay?
options: To explore different sides of an issue before reaching a balanced conclusion
To tell a story with a twist ending
questions.answer: To explore different sides of an issue before reaching a balanced conclusion

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which feature is most typical of a newspaper or magazine article?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: In an article, what term describes the short sub-heading under the headline that adds detail?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Who is the most likely audience for an article titled 'Five Revision Tricks That Actually Work' in a teen magazine?
questions.hint: Look at the topic and where it is published.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which phrase best signals a counter-argument in a discursive essay?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which register is most suitable for a discursive essay written for an examiner?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What term describes a question asked for effect, not expecting an answer, often used to engage readers of articles?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: A review says: 'The plot drags, but the soundtrack is breathtaking.' What does this show about the writer's approach?
options: It gives a balanced judgement with both criticism and praise
It is written in the second person
questions.answer: It gives a balanced judgement with both criticism and praise

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which of these is most likely to appear in the conclusion of a discursive essay?
options: A weighed-up final view that considers both sides
A brand-new argument never mentioned before
questions.answer: A weighed-up final view that considers both sides
questions.hint: A conclusion should not introduce new points.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Why might an article writer use direct quotations from an invented expert, such as 'Dr Lena Okafor, a sleep scientist'?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: How does the purpose of a review differ from that of an article?
options: A review mainly evaluates something; an article may inform, explain or argue about a topic
A review always tells a story; an article never has opinions
They have exactly the same purpose
questions.answer: A review mainly evaluates something; an article may inform, explain or argue about a topic

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which sentence uses the direct address typical of an article written to persuade teenagers?
options: You might think you're too busy to volunteer, but think again.
The volunteers arrived at nine o'clock.
Volunteering was established in many towns.
It is said that some people volunteer.
questions.answer: You might think you're too busy to volunteer, but think again.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Explain how the audience of a text might affect the language a writer chooses. Refer to one non-fiction form in your answer.
questions.hint: Think about vocabulary, tone and formality.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Compare the purpose and structure of a review and a discursive essay. Give at least two differences.
questions.hint: Consider what each text is trying to achieve and how it is organised.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: A writer is producing an article for a school website arguing that homework should be reduced. Explain two techniques they could use to engage a teenage audience, and why each would work.
questions.hint: Think about tone, address and evidence.

en_lit.topic: Short stories: culture and context — 'Sale' (Desai) and 'Smoke' (Mehta)

The number of pages in a story
The font used to print a story

It means the setting is unimportant

questions.subject: en_lit

It removes the need for characters
It shows the story is a comedy

questions.subject: en_lit
